q: Cuttings brought from France in 1853 by an agronomist hired to modernise Mendoza's farming gave the country its emblem. Which red variety was it?
exp: Michel Aime Pouget was engaged to run a new agricultural school and arrived with French vine material. Malbec reached Argentina before phylloxera had reshaped its French homeland.

q: Set beside Cahors, the Malbec grown in Mendoza differs as a plant in which way?
opts: Much larger berries in looser bunches
exp: A century and a half of selection in a dry, sunny place produced a distinct plant. More skin per unit of juice is part of why Argentine Malbec is plusher and darker than the French original.

q: DNA analysis showed Argentina's most aromatic white to be a natural cross of Criolla Chica with which other variety?
exp: Criolla Chica is the missionaries' vine, called Pais in Chile and Mission in California. The Muscat parent accounts for the flowery, grapey perfume of Torrontes.

q: A guest expects sweetness from a heady, rose-scented Argentine white and meets a dry, faintly bitter finish instead. Which variety was poured?
exp: Perfume and sugar are separate things, and this is the standing proof. The grip on the finish is characteristic and makes the wine a better match for spiced food than its nose suggests.

q: A red planted second only to Malbec in Argentina carries an Italian name, yet DNA matched it to Savoie's Douce Noire. Which is it?
exp: The same vine is called Charbono in California. Argentine Bonarda ripens late and gives juicy dark fruit with soft tannin, and it is only now being taken seriously.

q: Pink-skinned varieties still cover a wide stretch of Argentine vineyard and supply inexpensive wine for the home market. Which pair are they?
exp: Both descend from the vines the Spanish brought and both crop heavily. Their acreage has fallen steadily as growers replant to Malbec for export.

q: Century-old plantings of a Bordeaux white survive on the Rio Negro valley floor, a legacy of the settlers who first irrigated it. Which variety?
exp: Patagonian Semillon is lean and long lived, nothing like the broad versions the grape gives in warmer places. Old Merlot and Pinot Noir survive alongside it.

q: Between the coastal range and the Andes runs a long structural depression that lends its name to the heart of Chilean viticulture. What is that name?
exp: In Chilean law the Valle Central covers Maipo, Rapel, Curico and Maule. Casablanca and Aconcagua sit outside it, in the Aconcagua region further north.

q: A cold ocean current running north along the shore drags fog inland each morning and keeps Chilean coastal vineyards far cooler than their latitude suggests. Which current?
exp: It carries Antarctic water up the western seaboard and is the single largest cooling influence on Chilean wine. Without it these latitudes would be far too warm for Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Noir.

q: Dense sea fog that rolls into the far northern valleys at dawn carries a local name. Which?
exp: In Limari and Elqui the camanchaca is what makes viticulture possible so near the Atacama. It burns off by mid-morning and leaves a fiercely sunny afternoon behind it.

q: Rainfall across Chile's wine country changes steadily along the length of the country. In which direction does it increase?
opts: It changes very little from one end to the other
It peaks in the middle and falls away at both ends
exp: The north shades into the Atacama desert and the far south is genuinely wet. That gradient is why irrigation is compulsory in Limari and optional or unnecessary in Itata.

q: Chilean labels may add Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes beside the valley name. What do those three words tell a buyer?
opts: The sweetness of the finished wine
Where it sits between ocean and mountains
How long the wine spent in oak
exp: The three words place the vineyard between the ocean and the mountains. Introduced in 2011, they cut across the north-south valley names, which had lumped cool coastal fruit in with warm inland fruit. Costa is the maritime side, Andes the mountain side, Entre Cordilleras the ground between.

q: Almost every Chilean vine grows on its own roots rather than on grafted rootstock. Which fact allows it?
opts: Chilean law forbids the import of rootstock
Drip irrigation drowns the louse in the root zone
Chilean vines are hybrids the louse cannot feed on
Phylloxera has never taken hold in the country
exp: Desert to the north, ocean to the west, the Andes to the east and cold to the south have kept the pest out. Ungrafted vines are the ordinary case here and a rarity almost everywhere else.

q: Vineyards in Chile's northern and central valleys cannot carry a crop on growing-season rainfall alone. What waters them?
opts: River water fed by Andean snowmelt
Desalinated seawater piped from the coast
Artesian springs in the coastal range
exp: A Mediterranean climate puts its rain in winter, so the vine is driest exactly when it is growing. Meltwater arrives in the rivers as the season warms, which is convenient timing.

q: Gravel terraces on the upper reaches of a river immediately south of Santiago produce Chile's most celebrated Cabernet Sauvignon. Which valley?
exp: Maipo Cabernet is often marked by a minty, eucalyptus lift over blackcurrant fruit. The valley runs from the Andes nearly to the sea, and the Andean end is the serious part.

q: The flagship Cabernets of Alto Maipo come overwhelmingly from one commune on stony ground beside the river. Which?
exp: Puente Alto and neighbouring Pirque sit high on the Maipo's alluvial gravels, close enough to the Andes to catch cold night air draining off the mountains.
